name: Describe the agentic loop of an AI coding agent. Name its components, explain what each does, and say what a typical run looks like (who chooses each step, what a failing test means, what the human does).
answer: You give the agent a task in natural language (e.g. “add rate limiting to the upload endpoint, keep the existing tests green”). The agent then runs a loop: plan → act → observe → verify, repeated until done. The model is the reasoning engine that chooses the next step. The context is what the model sees: the prompt, the repository, docs and memory. Tools are how it acts: shell, files, tests, git, MCP servers. The harness is the scaffold that runs the loop. Verification (tests, linters, review) closes the loop and decides whether to continue or finish with a pull request. The trace records reasoning, actions and observations. In a typical run every step is a tool call chosen by the model, not scripted; a failing test is not a bug report but the next instruction; and the human’s job starts at “open pull request”: reading the diff and the trace.
keyPoints: Loop: plan → act → observe → verify; not done → next step, done → pull request
Model = reasoning engine; context = prompt, repo, docs, memory
Tools = shell, files, tests, git, MCP servers; harness = scaffold running the loop
Verification (tests, linters, review) closes the loop; trace = record of reasoning, actions, observations
Every step is a tool call chosen by the model; a failing test becomes the next instruction
The human reviews the diff and the trace, not the keystrokes

name: “Agent is NOT only the model.” Explain what decisions an engineer has to make in each part of the agentic loop.
answer: Every box of the loop requires engineering decisions, not just the choice of a model. Model: which one, at what cost, and for which step – a planner and a code editor need not be the same model. Context: what to put in front of the model, what to leave out and when to summarise, because the window is finite and attention is not uniform. Tools: what the agent may call, with which permissions and in which sandbox. Harness: how many retries, when to stop, when to ask a human, and how to record the trace. Verification: which signal closes the loop – and what happens when the tests themselves are what is wrong.
keyPoints: Model: which model, cost, possibly different models for different steps
Context: what to include/leave out, when to summarise; window finite, attention not uniform
Tools: allowed calls, permissions, sandbox
Harness: retries, stopping, asking a human, recording the trace
Verification: what closes the loop, and what if the tests are wrong

name: Describe the five stages from autocomplete to multi-agent systems. What changes as you go down the list?
answer: (1) Completion predicts the next tokens in the editor; you keep every decision. (2) Chat: you paste code, it answers, you copy back; it has no access to your environment. (3) Agent in the IDE reads and edits files and runs commands while you approve steps. (4) Background agent takes a task, works in its own sandbox and returns a pull request. (5) Multi-agent: one agent plans and delegates to others, with shared memory and specialised roles. Going down the list changes who decides, what the model can touch, and how much you see before it acts. Tools available today sit at levels 3 and 4; the course considers mostly 3–5.
keyPoints: Completion: predicts the next tokens in the editor; you keep every decision
Chat: you paste code and copy the answer back; no access to your environment
Agent in the IDE: reads and edits files, runs commands; you approve steps
Background agent: works alone in its own sandbox and returns a pull request
Multi-agent: one agent plans and delegates to specialised agents with shared memory
Down the list: who decides, what the model can touch, how much you see before it acts

name: What are the main features of agentic development, and how does the work of a software engineer change because of it?
answer: In agentic development specification replaces implementation as the main human output (constraints, acceptance criteria, examples), and tests become the interface to the agent – a failing test is an instruction it can act on. Work can run in parallel (several agents on several branches, humans review), systems are composable (sub-agents, reusable skills, MCP tool servers, shared memory), and the loop self-corrects by retrying on failure without a human in between. For the engineer this means less typing of implementations, less reading docs to recall an API, less boilerplate and less waiting on one serial task – and more writing of specifications the loop can act on, designing the tests that define “done”, reviewing diffs and traces, deciding what the agent may touch, and knowing when the output is wrong.
keyPoints: Specification (constraints, acceptance criteria, examples) replaces implementation
Tests are the interface: a failing test is an instruction
Parallelism, composability (sub-agents, skills, MCP, memory), self-correction
Less: typing code, recalling APIs, boilerplate, waiting on serial tasks
More: specs, designing tests, reviewing diffs/traces, deciding permissions, spotting wrong output

name: “Nothing in the loop is new.” Which parts of the development loop were already automated before AI agents (around 2015), and which step was not? Why does that matter for today’s agents?
answer: By 2015 developers already ran the loop by hand – read the ticket, edit, run the tests, read the failure, fix, push – and everything around the human was automated: CI ran the test suite on every push and reported failures, linters and type checkers gated the merge, codemods rewrote thousands of call sites mechanically, and bots opened pull requests (e.g. dependency bumps) and let CI judge them. The one step never automated was reading the failure and deciding what to do next: CI could say which tests were red, but only a person could work out what caused it, often something other than the edited code. That step is what the model now does – the progress in models is what made it good enough to close the loop.
keyPoints: The loop (ticket → edit → test → read failure → fix → push) was already standard practice
Automated already: CI, linters/type checkers, codemods, bots opening PRs
Not automated: interpreting the failure and deciding the next step
That step is the model; models got good enough to close the loop

name: Explain why neural networks were considered a dead end around 2010 and what changed in 2012. What general pattern do you see in the development of AI since then?
answer: Around 2010, SVMs, random forests and gradient boosting won competitions, and feature engineering was the key skill. Neural networks faced two objections: they were too complex (a black box with no theory of generalisation, unlike SVM margins or forest feature importances) and not powerful enough (hard to train: vanishing gradients, sigmoids, no good initialisation). Both objections were correct then. In 2012 a deep network (AlexNet) won the ImageNet challenge by a large margin over the best classical pipeline (top-5 error about 15 % vs 26 %). Its recipe – a large labelled data set, two consumer GPUs, eight layers, ReLU and dropout – contained nothing new on its own; it worked because the pieces came together at scale. This removed the second objection; the first (we cannot read the weights) still holds. Within a few years every entry was a deep net, and learned representations replaced hand-designed features. The pattern since then: more data, more compute, and one idea that lets them be used together – each time an engineered pipeline is replaced by a learned one once the scale is there (learned features beat engineered ones in 2012; around 2020 one model trained on everything beat a model per task). The Transformer, for example, is not smarter than older networks, just easier to scale, because its training parallelises.
keyPoints: 2010: shallow models plus hand-engineered features dominated
Objections: black box (still true) and hard to train (overcome in 2012)
2012: a deep net clearly beat classical pipelines – data, GPUs and simple tricks together at scale
Pattern: data + compute + one enabling idea; learned replaces engineered once scale exists
Transformer: not smarter, just easier to scale (parallel training)

name: What made reinforcement learning in game playing (e.g. AlphaGo, AlphaZero) work, and how does this connect to how today’s coding models are trained?
answer: AlphaGo (2016) beat a top professional Go player with a learned policy and value network guiding tree search, trained on human games and then self-play; AlphaZero (2017) used no human games at all, only self-play from the rules. What made this possible was a verifiable signal (you win or lose), cheap to compute, and a loop that runs millions of times without a human. This is sometimes summarised as “closed world, cheap verifier, let the loop run” – which is how models are trained on code today, and it is the agentic loop with the human removed. Around 2024–25 reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1) applied reinforcement learning to tasks with a verifier (maths, code), and models were trained for tool use and whole agentic trajectories: the 2019 game-playing recipe met the 2020 language model.
keyPoints: AlphaGo: policy/value network + tree search, human games then self-play; AlphaZero: self-play only
Key ingredients: verifiable signal, cheap to compute, loop without a human
Same recipe trains models on code today (tests as verifier)
Reasoning models: RL on tasks with a verifier; models trained for tool use / agentic trajectories

name: Describe the four stages of AI coding tools. Along which dimensions do they differ?
answer: (1) Completion from static analysis (IntelliSense 1996, IntelliJ/Eclipse, today language servers/LSP): the IDE parses your program and lists what can go after a dot – deterministic and never wrong about a name, but with no idea what you mean; you choose. (2) Generation from data (TabNine, Codex/Copilot 2021): code is “natural” and predictable, so a model learned from everyone’s code completes lines and whole functions, automating the copy-and-adapt loop from Stack Overflow. (3) Models that read your code base (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, Cursor, Copilot Chat): conversation in the editor with the repository as context; but no feedback – the model cannot run anything, you verify. (4) Agents (Devin, Claude Code, Codex, 2024–25): the model gets a shell, runs the tests, reads the failure and edits again. The stages differ in where knowledge comes from (your code → everyone’s code → both), who decides (you → the model → the loop) and feedback (none → the tests).
keyPoints: 1 static analysis (IntelliSense, LSP): exact but no intent
2 generation from data (TabNine, Copilot): everyone’s code, copy-and-adapt automated
3 models reading your repo (chat, Cursor): context but no feedback
4 agents: shell, run tests, iterate
Knowledge: yours → everyone’s → both; decision: you → model → loop; feedback: none → tests

name: Benchmark numbers suggest AI coding tools work very well. Name four things these numbers do not tell you and explain each briefly. What follows for using the tools on your own tasks?
answer: (1) They work less often than the demo suggests: benchmark tasks are short, self-contained and come with tests that define “done”, unlike most real tasks; on harder, more realistic benchmarks the same models solve far fewer tasks; task length matters most – the length an agent completes reliably is several times shorter than the length it completes half the time; and failure is quiet: the agent stops with a plausible diff and green tests it wrote itself. (2) They do not make you faster the way it feels: in a randomised trial, developers felt faster with AI but were measured slower. (3) They can be turned against you: the agent reads untrusted text while holding real credentials, so instructions hidden in that text can act with your rights. (4) They change what you learn: in a randomised trial of developers learning an unfamiliar library, the AI group had no average productivity gain but scored clearly lower on a later comprehension test taken without AI, worst on debugging; those who leaned on it hardest finished fastest and understood least, while asking it for explanations cost nothing (limits: one library, mostly junior developers, immediate comprehension). Reviewing a diff or judging a trace rests on skills you get by doing the work. Conclusion: the loop works on tasks you can specify and verify, at lengths you can check, in code you understand. Outside that it fails quietly, feels productive and is exposed to anyone who can get text in front of it – and where that boundary runs for your task, code base and tool, no benchmark tells you: you have to measure it yourself.
keyPoints: Work less often than demos: benchmark tasks are short and well-tested; harder benchmarks score much lower; failure is quiet
Feel faster than they are: perceived and measured speed disagree
Can be turned against you: untrusted text plus your credentials
Change what you learn: heavy reliance lowers comprehension, especially debugging; asking for explanations does not
Works on specifiable, verifiable, checkable tasks in code you understand; measure the boundary yourself

name: Describe the randomised controlled trial on developer productivity with AI (METR, 2025): experienced open-source developers worked on real issues in their own repositories, and for each issue AI use was allowed or forbidden at random. What did it find, and what explains the result?
answer: Setup: 16 experienced open-source developers and about 250 real issues in repositories they knew well; randomising per issue makes the issues with and without AI comparable. Finding: before the study the developers expected to be faster with AI (by about a quarter), and afterwards they still believed they had been faster (by about a fifth) – but measured, they were slower (by about a fifth). The feeling of speed and the measurement disagreed by roughly 40 percentage points. Explanation: the time went into prompting, waiting, and reviewing and fixing output that was almost right; and the developers knew their code base far better than the model did, so the model’s knowledge of “everyone’s code” added little to their knowledge of “their code”. Earlier studies with large speed-ups used small greenfield tasks in unfamiliar code – exactly the setting where the model’s general knowledge beats the developer’s. Caveat: the result holds for the tools of early 2025. A follow-up with newer tools suggested a speed-up, but its range includes zero, and the design broke down because many developers no longer wanted to do tasks without AI – for current tools there is no clean measurement.
keyPoints: Randomised per issue; experienced developers in their own repositories
Developers expected and afterwards believed they were faster; measured, they were slower
Perception and measurement can disagree widely – measure, do not rely on feeling
Time lost on prompting, waiting, reviewing and fixing almost-right output
Familiar code favours the developer; earlier speed-ups came from greenfield, unfamiliar tasks
Holds for early-2025 tools; no clean measurement for newer ones

name: Explain why prompt injection is a serious risk for coding agents, and why the risk grows with autonomy. Illustrate it with this scenario: an agent that has access to a user's repositories reads a public GitHub issue written by a stranger.
answer: An agent reads untrusted text – issues, web pages, dependencies, comments – while holding real credentials: your shell, your git, your tokens. Text it reads can contain instructions, and the model cannot reliably tell data from commands; this is prompt injection. In a real case from 2025, a public GitHub issue told an agent with repository access to “help” by summarising the user’s private repositories into a public pull request – and it did. The failure modes now have names (OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications: goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, memory poisoning, rogue agents). Every step down the autonomy ladder widens what a single bad instruction can reach.
keyPoints: Agent reads untrusted text and holds credentials (shell, git, tokens)
Model cannot reliably separate data from instructions
Example: public issue made an agent leak private repos into a public PR
Failure modes are now catalogued (OWASP agentic list): goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, memory poisoning, rogue agents
More autonomy → a bad instruction reaches further

name:
A simple learned model scores pull requests: \(\text{risk} = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b\), where \(x_1\) is the size of the change in hundreds of lines and \(x_2\) the number of tests added; a positive score means “will cause a bug”, a negative one “fine”. The current weights are \(w_1 = 1.0\), \(w_2 = -0.5\), \(b = -1.0\).
(a) Compute the risk of a 300-line PR with two tests and say what the model predicts.
(b) This PR in fact caused no bug, so the score should have been negative. Do one learning step with learning rate 0.1, in which every weight moves against the error in proportion to its own input (the bias has input 1): \(w_i \leftarrow w_i - 0.1 \cdot x_i\). Give the new weights and the new score of the same PR.
(c) What do the signs and sizes of the weights mean, and where do the weights come from?
answer:
(a) Score. With \(x_1 = 3\) and \(x_2 = 2\): \[\text{risk} = 1.0 \cdot 3 - 0.5 \cdot 2 - 1.0 = 1.0\] Positive, so the model predicts “will cause a bug” – wrong, because the PR was fine.
(b) One learning step. The score was too high, so each weight moves down by the learning rate times its own input: \[w_1 = 1.0 - 0.1 \cdot 3 = 0.7,\quad w_2 = -0.5 - 0.1 \cdot 2 = -0.7,\quad b = -1.0 - 0.1 \cdot 1 = -1.1\] The weight with the largest input (\(w_1\), which pushed the score up hardest) moves most. New score: \[0.7 \cdot 3 - 0.7 \cdot 2 - 1.1 = -0.4\] Negative – the PR is now on the right side. (A simplified illustration: real training also scales the step by how wrong the output was.)
(c) Meaning. The weights are readable: the sign says in which direction an input pushes the risk (bigger change → more risk, each test → less risk), the size says how much, and \(b\) is the starting point for a tiny PR with no tests. Geometrically, \(\text{risk} = 0\) is a line separating risky from fine PRs; \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) tilt it, \(b\) shifts it, and learning moves and rotates it. The weights come from data: past PRs with known outcomes, each nudging the weights a little. The data is the specification; nobody sets the weights by hand.
keyPoints: Score: \(1.0 \cdot 3 - 0.5 \cdot 2 - 1.0 = 1.0\) → predicts a bug (wrong)
Update rule: each weight moves against the error by learning rate × its own input
New score: \(0.7 \cdot 3 - 0.7 \cdot 2 - 1.1 = -0.4\) → now correct
Sign = direction, size = strength; \(\text{risk} = 0\) is a separating line
Weights are learned from data with known outcomes, not set by hand

name: What carries over from a simple weighted-sum model (a few readable weights learned from labelled examples) to a large neural network with around \(10^{12}\) weights, and what does not? What is engineered by people and what is learned?
answer:
The object. A neural network takes a vector of numbers and returns a vector of numbers. In between are many copies of one simple device, the neuron, arranged in layers: each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, applies a fixed non-linear function (e.g. ReLU, which sets negatives to zero) and outputs one number. All the behaviour is in the weights – there may be around \(10^{12}\) of them.
What carries over. The same weighted sums and the same learning loop: compare the output with a target from the data and nudge every weight a small step towards it, one example after another; a weight learns only from what is in the data. At scale the data is web text, the target is the next word, and the nudge for each weight is computed automatically by backpropagation.
What does not. You can no longer read the weights. In the small model a negative weight on “tests added” means “tests reduce risk”; in a large model a single weight somewhere in layer 61 means nothing on its own – the “black box” objection from 2010 still holds.
Engineered vs learned. People choose the data, what counts as the target, how big a step to take and when to stop; the weights themselves are learned.
keyPoints: Neuron = weighted sum + fixed non-linearity (ReLU); behaviour lives in the weights
Same learning loop: small steps towards targets taken from the data
At scale: web text, next-word target, backpropagation computes the nudges
Individual weights are no longer interpretable (black box)
Engineered: data, target, step size, stopping; learned: the weights
